instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
output: mtron has three categories of types. Mono types: bool (true/false), int (integers), real (floating point), str (strings), uri (uniform resource identifiers), bytes (binary data). Poly types: rec (records/maps with key-value pairs), lst (lists/sequences). Call types: inst (instructions with domain/range), code (executable code blocks). Types are structural and Turing Complete using [?predicate] refinement. Base types have tid == vid (e.g. int::T@int).

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: What is the difference between tid and vid in mtron?
output: In mtron, every Obj has a tid (Type ID) and vid (Value ID). For a type: vid is the type's name (e.g. 'nat') and tid is its refinement (e.g. 'int' giving int::T[?>0]@nat). For a value: vid is the value's location in space (e.g. nat::29@/usr/marko/age) and tid is the type constraining it. tid == vid for base types, creating loops in the identifier chain.

the four ways a spelling becomes an address

They are distinct, and knowing which is which is most of the uri grammar:

| spelling     | resolved by                                                         | declared by                                                                                         |
|--------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| math:cos   | an isa prefix — a scheme with no host names a vocabulary        | import(/m/math, math); the table is *</instset/prefix>                                          |
| //ginger/a | a network name — a host with no scheme and no port names a peer | /network/prefix -> [//ginger => <ws://ginger.local:8555>], or </network/prefix/ginger> by label |
| cos        | a redirect — the short name an address already has              | derived from what is mounted; *</memory/redirect>                                                 |
| /mcp       | a route — a path prefix a space serves                          | the space's own route field, e.g. http_server::[route=>[/mcp => mcp_mtron]]                     |

big() / small() covers the first three: a primordial uri helper at metatron's own level, for humans. A space's
route is not part of it — a space routes the addresses it serves, on its own behalf.

And a rewrite is none of these: it is the compiler's code-transform rule (instSet.rewrites()), a different word
for
a different thing. When in doubt: a rewrite changes *code*, a redirect changes *what a name means*.

the words, one line each

The vocabulary above is small and every term is load-bearing, so the confusions are specific. These are the ones that
have actually cost someone an afternoon.

addresses

| term            | means                                                                                                  |
|-----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| vid           | where a value lives (nat::29@/usr/marko/age → the vid is /usr/marko/age)                           |
| tid           | the type constraining it (the same value's tid is int)                                               |
| origin        | a service's full address: scheme://host:port. The unit peers are keyed by and dialed at              |
| authority     | host:port — an origin without the scheme. hasAuthority() demands both host and port            |
| host          | the host alone. The wire's gate: an address with a host is *someone else's to answer* (Network.read) |
| isPrefixed()  | scheme, no host — the vocabulary's slot (math:cos)                                                   |
| isAddressed() | just hasHost() — says nothing about ports or schemes                                                 |
| isHosted()    | host, no scheme, no port — the network name slot (//ginger/a)                                    |
| noobj         | the empty answer. A read that matches nothing returns it; a write of it is the universal close         |

reach and knowledge

| term               | means                                                                              |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| roster           | what the system knows: <host> => uri{+}, connectionless. Shared at the root  |
| peer             | what this machine has dialed: one member per surface, keyed by the dial's path |
| listener         | what it answers on: the sockets it serves, and therefore what mDNS announces   |
| prefix (network) | what you call it: <label> => origin, one listing at the root                 |
| reach              | dialed peers — per frame, retractable, not inherited                           |
| denotation         | what a spelling means — machine-global, inherited, never scoped                    |

structure and process

| term               | means                                                                                             |
|--------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| space            | a subset of the graph one address pattern serves (memspace::[pattern=>/usr/#])                  |
| route            | a space's own path→target table, applied when it serves a read or write                       |
| mount / import | making a space or an instruction set available (InstSet.mount, @vid writes)                   |
| frame            | a child machine: push/pop are the call stack, move chooses a machine without closing one    |
| redirect         | a short name's home, big()/small(). Exposed at *</memory/redirect>, rewritable deliberately |
| prefix (isa)     | a vocabulary's short scheme, bound by the import that mounted it                                  |
| rewrite          | a compiler rule over code. Not a name, not an address — it transforms programs                |

The rule of thumb: an address is *declared* (a prefix, a name, a route's key), a redirect is *derived* from what was
mounted, and a rewrite is *code*.

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Explain the mtron concept: code pattern matching.
output:
Code is data. A poly holds code without running it ([plus(1).mult(2)]), and ==[...] applies an instruction to that
code as a value. update() (sugar'd >>=) to code changes the runs of instructions a pattern matches, as
update() on a str changes the sections a regex matches.

A code pattern is code whose parts are tests. The code tests the pattern, as a value tests a type:

* an instruction's name is a uri pattern: </m/inst/{plus,mult}> matches either (branching uris), # matches
  any.
* an argument is the type it must be: int::T is one int, int{*}::T a bag of them, int::T[?>0] a positive int.
* a predicate guards an argument (plus(?>0)), a literal matches itself (plus(2)), and an instruction pattern
  nests (mult(#(mult(_))) matches a mult whose argument is any instruction holding a mult).

mtron> [plus(1).mult(2).plus(3)]==[>>=[plus(int::T)=>mult(5)]]                              [-- every match changes --]
==>[mult(5).mult(2).mult(5)]
mtron> [plus(1).plus(2).mult(3)]==[>>=[plus(int::T).plus(int::T)=>plus(3)]]                 [-- a run matches as a whole --]
==>[plus(3).mult(3)]
mtron> [plus(1).mult(2).plus(3)]==[>>=[</m/inst/{plus,mult}>(int::T)=>id()]]                [-- a uri pattern names the inst --]
==>[id().id().id()]
mtron> [start({1,2}).plus(1)]==[>>=[start(int::T)=>start(0)]]                               [-- int{2}::T is not int::T unchanged --]
==>[start({1,2}).plus(1)]
mtron> [start({1,2}).plus(1)]==[>>=[start(int{*}::T)=>start(0)]]                            [-- int{*} takes the bag --]
==>[start(0).plus(1)]
mtron> [mult(1).plus(2).mult(3)]==[>>=[plus(int::T).mult(int::T)=>[mult(int::T)=>mult(7)]]] [-- a rec changes inside the run --]
==>[mult(1).plus(2).mult(7)]
A pattern matches runs of consecutive instructions, left to right, never overlapping. A code change replaces the run,
and a rec applies its own rules inside the run. The rules run in order, each over what the last one left, and a change
is not matched again.

in place: an instruction's args

A rule keyed by args (a uri, not a pattern) updates the arguments of each instruction in place, as >>= updates a
lst: a call transforms, a literal or a blocked |x replaces, _ keeps a value, #::T keeps an argument that is itself
an instruction, and the rule's lst gives the new arity. An instruction updates itself the same way
(update?inst<=inst(rec::T)).

mtron> [plus(5)]==[>>=[args=>[+10]]]                                    [-- an inst updates its own args --]
==>[plus(15)]
mtron> [branch(plus(1),mult(2))]==[>>=[args=>[#::T,|mult(3)]]]          [-- keep one, replace the other --]
==>[branch(plus(1),mult(3))]
mtron> [plus(5).mult(2)]==[>>=[plus(int::T)=>[args=>[+10]]]]            [-- in place, in the run a pattern matched --]
==>[plus(15).mult(2)]
names and templates

@name on a pattern element names what it matched. In a change, a ${...} argument is a template parameter: it is
evaluated against what the run holds in that place, it reads the names with *name, and its value (not its text) is
the argument. Nest one template inside another by alternating ${...} and {{{...}}}. Everything outside a template
parameter is literal: plus(+5) stays plus(plus(5)).

mtron> [plus(5).mult(2)]==[>>=[plus(int::T)=>plus(${+10})]]                                             [-- evaluated against the 5 --]
==>[plus(15).mult(2)]
mtron> [plus(5).mult(2)]==[>>=[plus(int::T@a)=>plus(${*a.plus(10)})]]                                   [-- a named group --]
==>[plus(15).mult(2)]
mtron> [plus(2).plus(3).mult(4)]==[>>=[plus(int::T@a).plus(int::T@b)=>plus(${*a.plus(*b)})]]            [-- the plus monoid law, as data --]
==>[plus(5).mult(4)]
mtron> [mult(plus(mult(3))).plus(1)]==[>>=[mult(#(mult(int::T@k)))=>mult(plus(mult(${*k.mult(2)})))]]   [-- a name bound at depth --]
==>[mult(plus(mult(6))).plus(1)]
The names are the change's own argument uris: a frame on the thread's argument stack, pushed for the change and popped
after it, so threads never see each other's names. A name on a typed hole is also a type of the machine.
int::T@a defines a::T in the machine's root frame (the scope of relative uris), and a later plain int::T@a refers
to whatever a already is. So:

* within one machine, a name means one type: reuse @a only for the same type, and give a different refinement its
  own name.
* threads that pattern-match concurrently each work in a machine of their own (push, then pop). Their types live
  and die there; in one shared machine their definitions collide.
* a name the argument stack itself answers (such as q) cannot be read back as a capture.

input: What is core concepts in mtron?

vid and tid

Every type in mtron is defined by two URIs:

| Component | Meaning                               | Example                             |
|-----------|---------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| tid   | The type being refined (its base) | rec in rec::T[?[age=>int::T]]   |
| vid   | The type being defined/named      | person in rec::T[?[...]]@person |

For values (instances), the roles are analogous:

- tid = the value's type (what kind of thing it is)
- vid = the value's location in space (its address/identity)

person::[name=>'marko',age=>29]@marko
  ^^^^^                          ^^^^^
  tid (what it is)               vid (where it is)
the ::T suffix

::T lifts an object to the type-of that object. int::T means "the type of integers." person::T means "the type
named person."

Without ::T, int is a value (the integer zero). int::0 is a typed value (an integer zero). int::T is the integer
type itself.

base types (nominal)

The built-in primitive types. Every type ultimately refines one of these. Base types are nominal — their tid equals
their vid (e.g., int::T = int::T@int). There is nothing structural distinguishing an int from a str save the
name:

| Type       | URI        | Cardinality | Description                |
|------------|------------|-------------|----------------------------|
| int::T   | /m/int   | 1           | 64-bit signed integer      |
| real::T  | /m/real  | 1           | 64-bit IEEE 754 float      |
| str::T   | /m/str   | 1           | UTF-8 string               |
| bool::T  | /m/bool  | 1           | true / false               |
| uri::T   | /m/uri   | 1           | fURI reference             |
| bytes::T | /m/bytes | 1           | raw byte array             |
| rec::T   | /m/rec   | 1           | record (key-value map)     |

| rel::T   | /m/rel   | 1           | relation (key=>value pair) |
| inst::T  | /m/inst  | 1           | instruction (function)     |

| int{*}::T   | {0,∞}    | zero or more (maybe some) |

input: Define type definition as used in mtron.

creating a type

A type is created with tid::T[predicate][constructor]@vid — a bare statement; the predicate, the constructor, and the
vid are each optional, and a type without a vid is a lambda (ephemeral) type:

creating types
mtron> import(/m/math,math)      [-- module import, namespaced math — its types read math:nat, math:minute, ... --]
mtron> int::T[is(gt(0))]@posint  [-- a new member of the hierarchy: integers greater than zero --]
mtron> posint::T[is(gt(100))]@hundreds
mtron> int::T[is(gt(0))][mult(10)]@int2x
mtron> rec::T[?[name=>str::T,age=>int::T]]@being
A created type is first-class: it refines (posint refines int), is refined (hundreds refines posint), builds
values under its own name, and other values can be cast onto it. The stock types the VM ships with (base types,
person, and the module types the boot loads) are created the same way — you just don't spell the creation.

One distinction that matters: xxx -> <type> is *not* type creation. The arrow writes a type value to the uri
/xxx — a reference (an alias) that takes over the short name for value lookups (*xxx) — while type references
(xxx::T) still resolve to the real type when one exists. A refinement built on a bare reference with no type behind
it (xxx::T[?]@yyy) lands off the type hierarchy; types refine types, not references.

instantiation

mtron> hundreds::150                  [-- 150, checked against the whole predicate stack, stamped --]
==>hundreds::150
mtron> 23.as(posint::T)               [-- posint::23 --]
==>posint::23
mtron> being::[name=>'marko',age=>29] [-- a rec built under its type --]
==>being::[name=>'marko',age=>29]
mtron> int::42@the_answer             [-- a plain value, addressed in the space --]

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
output:
A predicate is a constraint that values must satisfy to be members of the type. Two families:

isa-predicates (structural)

Created with ?[...] — defines a required record structure (being, created above, is one of these):

mtron> rec::T[?[age=>int::T]]                              [-- a lambda type: a rec whose age field is an int --]
mtron> rec::T[?[name=>str::T, address=>str{?}::T]]         [-- address optional (str{?}::T) --]
mtron> rec::T[?[flag=>str{2}::T, member=>being{+}::T]]@roster
A field's type can be any type — including a lambda type or a created one like being.

Multi-level stacking: every refinement inherits the whole predicate stack of its ancestors, and the stack is
checked level by level:

mtron> [-- hundreds::T = [is(gt(100))] on top of posint's [is(gt(0))] on top of int --]
mtron> hundreds::150                [-- 150  (passes both levels) --]
==>hundreds::150
mtron> hundreds::50         [-- dies at posint's level — the ancestor stack is enforced, not just the top --]
==>fail::[parse error at line 1, col 1: 50 is not a posint::T[/m/inst/is(/m/inst/gt(100))]@hundreds
   	while parsing: hundreds::50]
non-isa predicates (nominal)

Freeform functional constraints using instructions:

mtron> int::T[is(gt(0))]
mtron> int::T[?>0]
mtron> int::T[?=42]
mtron> int::T[?>0.?<120]
The . operator chains predicates: p1.p2 means "apply p1, then apply p2 to the result." Both must succeed (AND
semantics).

OR semantics use split/merge:

mtron> [-- value must be > 0 OR < 120 --]
mtron> int::T[-<[?>0,?<120]>-]
predicate vs no predicate

A type without a predicate is the most general type at its level — it accepts any value with the correct base type
and coefficient:

mtron> int::T        [-- accepts any integer --]
mtron> int::T[?>0]   [-- only accepts positive integers --]
type constructors

A type can also carry a constructor — an instruction the type applies to values. The constructor sits alongside
the predicate in the type definition:

int::T[is(gt(0))][abs]@intabs
Two doors take a value through a type, and they treat the constructor differently.

Construction applies the constructor. type::value builds the value by running the constructor, so at this door
a negative is welcome — it is simply made positive on the way in (created below with an absolute-value constructor):

construction: type::value runs the constructor
mtron> int::T[is(gt(0))][-<|[is(lt(0)) => * -1, _ => _]>>]@intabs
mtron> intabs::-2                       [-- intabs::2  (the constructor ran on the way in) --]
==>intabs::2
mtron> intabs::2                        [-- intabs::2 --]
==>intabs::2
Casting tests first. .as(type) checks the predicate before the constructor gets a turn, so a value that cannot
fit is refused rather than coerced; a value that does fit still goes through the constructor:

casting: the predicate gates before the constructor
mtron> 2.isa(intabs::T)                 [-- 2  (the predicate admits it) --]
==>2
mtron> -2.isa(intabs::T)                [-- noobj  (the filter drops it: the verdict doubles as the output) --]
mtron> 2.as(intabs::T)                  [-- intabs::2  (admitted; the id branch of the ctor leaves it as-is) --]
==>intabs::2
mtron> -2.as(intabs::T)         [-- refused: the predicate tests before the constructor could run --]
==>fail::[inst apply failure: -2 is not a int::T[/m/inst/is(/m/inst/gt(0))][/m/inst/choose([/m/inst/is(/m/inst/lt(0))=>/m/inst/mult(-1),/m/inst/id()=>/m/inst/id()])./m/inst/rshift()]@intabs [structural] (at /m/inst/as@1)]
A converting constructor is visible the same way — it runs on the admitted value, and on nothing else:

a converting constructor (int2x, created above)
mtron> int2x::2                         [-- int2x::20  (the constructor mult(10) ran on the way in) --]
==>int2x::20
mtron> 2.as(int2x::T)                   [-- int2x::20  (admitted at the gate, then converted) --]
==>int2x::20
mtron> -2.as(int2x::T)          [-- refused for the same reason — the gate runs first --]
==>fail::[inst apply failure: -2 is not a int::T[/m/inst/is(/m/inst/gt(0))][/m/inst/mult(10)]@int2x [structural] (at /m/inst/as@1)]
A type with no constructor is a pure constraint — values must already satisfy the predicate to be members; there is
nothing to run them through.

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Explain the mtron concept: nominal vs structural types.
output:
The distinction depends solely on the existence of a predicate:

| Kind                       | Has predicate? | Has vid?         | Example                                              |
|----------------------------|----------------|------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| structural             | yes            | optional         | int::T[?>0]@posint — constraint defines membership |
| nominal                | no             | yes (tid ≠ vid)  | int::T@age — label defines membership              |
| base type (structural) | no             | yes (tid == vid) | int::T (= int::T@int) — primitive                |

- structural = any type with a predicate. The predicate specifies the structural requirements a value must satisfy.
  Isa predicates (?[...]) constrain record fields; non-isa predicates (is(gt(0))) constrain by computation.
- nominal (no predicate) = type distinguished purely by name/vid. When B::T == A::T structurally (same values) but
  have different vids, there exists only a nominal difference. A value of int::T@age is not the same type as a value
  of int::T@zipcode.
- base types are structural: int::T = int::T@int. An int is an int because of an internal structure outside
  the purview of the metatron vm.

A type can carry both a predicate and a VID: rec::T[?[age=>int::T]]@person. This type is structural (has a
predicate) AND named (has a VID). The predicate determines which values qualify; the vid allows nominal discrimination
from other structurally-identical types.

why nominal types matter

Structural types alone can over-match. A rec::T with name and age could represent both a human and a chicken. Nominal
types prevent this:

mtron> being::T@human                 [-- nominal siblings under being --]
mtron> being::T@chicken
mtron> [-- A human is NOT a chicken, despite identical structure --]
mtron> human::[name=>'marko',age=>29].as(chicken::T)
==>fail::[inst apply failure: human::[name=>'marko',age=>29] is not a being::T@chicken [nominal] (at /m/inst/as)]
This is the difference between experiential knowledge (structural — what can be observed) and authoritative
knowledge (nominal — what has been declared).

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Tell me about type hierarchy and refinement in mtron.
output:
Types form a tree rooted at #{*}::T (ALL). Each type has exactly one parent — the type its tid refines:

- If tid == vid (base type or self-referential): parent is #{*}::T
- Otherwise: parent is T(tid) — the base type being refined

hundreds::T  →  posint::T  →  int::T      (the int-branch, built above)
[is(gt(100))]   [is(gt(0))]   (base)
You can walk the hierarchy back to the root:

[-- the hierarchy walk — verified under a production VM boot --]
hundreds::T.type()                  [-- posint — the parent --]
hundreds::T.type().type()           [-- int --]
hundreds::T.repeat?<=int(code=>type(),until=>vid().?=#,emit=>true)
                                    [-- the whole chain, emitted one type per line, until the universal root --]

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Define pattern and generic types as used in mtron.
output:
URIs with wildcards create pattern types that match multiple concrete types:

| Pattern     | Matches                                           |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| #{*}::T   | everything (universal: any vid × any cardinality) |
| #::T      | any type vid (default cardinality {1})            |
| /m/+::T   | any base type under /m/                         |
| /m/+/+::T | any type two levels under /m/                   |
| int{*}::T | integers of any cardinality                       |
| int{?}::T | zero or one integer                               |

Generic types use polymorphic URIs — #{*}::T is the universal type that every value belongs to, which is why
it shows up in every contract: inst?rng=#{*}&dom=#{?}(<#>::T) reads "an instruction from maybe some of *any*
input to any output," and it is the notation ?docq prints for the insts you see everywhere in these docs:

mtron> 1.isa(#{*}::T)                   [-- 1  (every value is a citizen of the universal type) --]
==>1
mtron> 'mtron'.isa(#{*}::T)             [-- 'mtron' --]
==>'mtron'
mtron> int::T.isa(#{*}::T)              [-- noobj  (the isa rows admit values, not types) --]
Note the direction: values test against #{*}::T and pass, while type-vs-type — "is posint a refinement of
int?" — is asked of the type *hierarchy* (see *type hierarchy and refinement* above), not of a value.

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: What is poly types: three readings of the bracket in mtron?
output:
A type's bracket — the [...] after its name — has exactly one meaning per base type. The general category is poly
types; lst, rec and rel are its *readings*, not three words for the same construct.

the three readings

| construct    | name         | poly denotes                                                                                   | verb     |
|--------------|--------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------|
| lst[A,B]   | TENSOR TYPE  | the position types — the coordinates of an A × B (rank = bracket length, extent = the coefficient) | CONTAINS |
| rec[F1,F2] | FIBERED TYPE | the FIBERS (named, distinct objects)                                                           | EXPOSES  |
| rel[A,B,C] | PATH TYPE    | the vertices of the right-nested chain A => (B => C)                                         | CHAINS   |

graded says something about rank × extent — how many coordinates, and how far each one runs. It is a property of a
tensor, never a synonym for *poly*.

content vs object: why the readings do not collapse

The reading decides what the bracket's entries *are*, and that decides what a call does to the value.

A tensor's positions are the object's content. lst[int] is a list whose positions hold ints — it is not an
int. Position is the coordinate, so the type speaks about the value's own contents, one entry per position, and its
entries are not separate objects a call can reach: [29,'94103'] satisfies lst[age,zipcode]::T (position 0 is an
age, position 1 a zipcode) and fails lst[zipcode,age]::T, where the coordinates are swapped.
Two consequences, and they are the same consequence twice: there is no lifting *into* a tensor's positions (lst[int]
hands a call no second candidate), and a tensor's entries name no other type (lst[int] is never an int — a list of
ints is not an int). The coefficient is where extent lives, not another coordinate: lst[int{4}] is ONE position
holding four ints, while lst[int,int,int,int] is four positions.

A fibered type's entries are distinct objects. person[ninja] is a person *and* a ninja; the ninja is not the
bundle's content but an object the bundle exposes. So a value of that type is acceptable where ninja::T is
expected (its base or any fiber — see *acceptance and covariance*), and an instruction declared on ninja applies to
the fiber's value as if it had been declared top-level.

a bracket entry's coefficient: the multiplicity of the value AT that position or vertex

A bracket entry is a *position* (a tensor position, a path vertex), so a suffix coefficient is the multiplicity of the
value at that position — not another position, and not another hop. lst[int{2},str] is a two-position list whose
FIRST position holds two ints; rel[int,person{2}] is a two-vertex chain whose SECOND vertex holds two people
(1=>{bob,marko}, two people at that vertex — not two hops):

a suffix coefficient is the multiplicity of the value AT that position / vertex
mtron> wayfarer -> rec::T@wayfarer
mtron> lst[int{2},str]::[{1,2},'a']              [-- position 0 is an int{2}: one position, two ints --]
==>lst[int{2},str]::[{1,2},'a']
mtron> rel[int,wayfarer{2}]::(1=>{wayfarer::[name=>'bob'],wayfarer::[name=>'marko']})   [-- the second vertex holds two wayfarers --]
==>rel[int,wayfarer{2}]::(1=>{wayfarer::[name=>'bob'],wayfarer::[name=>'marko']})
mtron> lst[int{2},str]::[1,'a']          [-- one int is an int{1}: too few for an int{2} position --]
==>fail::[parse error at line 1, col 1: obj does not match /m/lst[/m/int{2},/m/str]::T
     [[1,'a']
         X=>
     lst[int{2},str]::T
     [X=>1,==>'a']]
     predicate apply failed on poly
   	while parsing: lst[int{2},str]::[1,'a']]
mtron> rel[int,wayfarer{2}]::(1=>wayfarer::[name=>'bob'])   [-- one wayfarer is too few for a wayfarer{2} vertex --]
==>fail::[parse error at line 1, col 1: obj does not match /m/rel[/m/int,wayfarer{2}]::T
     [1=>wayfarer::[name=>'bob']
         X=>
     rel[int,wayfarer{2}]::T
     [==>1,X=>wayfarer::[name=>'bob']]]
     predicate apply failed on poly
   	while parsing: rel[int,wayfarer{2}]::(1=>wayfarer::[name=>'bob'])]
The coefficient forms say how many values that position admits, exactly as they do anywhere else in a type:

| entry         | value at that position                                  |
|---------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| T / T{1}  | exactly one                                             |
| T{n}        | exactly n (lst[int{2},str] ⇒ [{1,2},'a'])           |
| T{n,m}      | an inclusive range — n, …, m                            |
| T{+}        | at least one, so the position is REQUIRED               |
| T{?}        | zero or one — ABSENT, or one that is still its type     |
| T{*}        | zero or more — absent is legal, and so is a multiplicity |

Absence is the zero end of the range, and it reads differently in the two readings. In a tensor the value is a
list, so a zero-admitting TRAILING position is one the shorter list does not fill — lst[str,int{?}] accepts ['a']. In
a path the value is a chain, so a zero-admitting VERTEX is one the chain omits — rel[int,wayfarer{?},str] accepts
1=>'tally' (the middle vertex skipped) while rel[int,wayfarer{+},str] does not. A present value must still be the
entry's type at both: {?} is zero-or-one, not "anything when present".

Not yet supported: a PREFIX coefficient, and repetition. lst[{4}int] — "the list is composed of four ints",
spelled before the entry rather than after it — is not matchable today. Neither is a position *repetition*: a suffix
coefficient judges the multiplicity of the value already at that position, and nothing reads it as "this entry
repeats, so the chain is longer" (whether a repeated vertex should lengthen a path is not settled). A NEGATIVE (anti)
coefficient is not a multiplicity at all, so a path reports it as not yet matched rather than judging it.

declaring a fibered type vs instantiating one

Three words, used consistently from here on:

- bundle — a value of a *fibered type*: the outer rec::T (person[ninja]::[…]). Formerly called the bundle.
- fiber — a particular field of that rec::T that its bracket LIFTS: the key/value becomes a virtual sibling of
  the rec's other fields, so an instruction can reach it as if it stood alone (role holding the ninja).
- field — any key=>value pair of a rec::T. Every fiber is a field; most fields are not fibers.

A fibered type is spelled twice, and the two brackets say different things:

rec[role,position]::T[?[name=>str::T, role=>rec::T, position=>rec::T]]@person
    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the DECLARATION's poly NAMES the fibers (field names)

person[ninja,position]::[...]
       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the INSTANCE's poly gives their TYPES (their contents)
- the DECLARATION's poly is a list of field names — the fibers this bundle exposes (its key range);
- the INSTANCE's poly is a list of type arguments — what each fiber's value is (its value range). A KEY belongs
  in the declaration's bracket, never the instance's: human[geo] would type a fiber with the key's own name.

The declaration's entries are parameters and the instance's are arguments, so resolution substitutes one for the
other positionally: person[role] + [ninja] → person[ninja], an unclaimed parameter keeps its declared entry, and
a request that names nothing leaves the declaration as it stands (Type.Helper.instantiate).

This asymmetry is why fURI.test — which compares names, never types — answers person[ninja].test(person[role])
as false: the lhs is a specialization and role is not the name ninja. The two are still related, at the type
layer, by that bound substitution rather than by the bracket claim.

lifting (dispatch into a fiber)

An instruction declared on a fiber's type applies to the fiber's VALUE as if it were top-level: fight?<=ninja() on a
person[ninja] bundle reaches the ninja object inside it, not the bundle.

Mechanically there is nothing trait-aware anywhere in the processor. The dispatch set is the BUNDLE plus the values
of its FIBERS, and each subject is selected and invoked on its own — so the "selection" is ordinary resolution, not
a lookup table keyed by the declaration:

- an untyped call lifts over all fibers; ?<=T selects one subject, because a named domain is the subject the
  call is about.
- a base-typed domain is about a subject's own form, never its name: ?<=rec(...) reaches the bundle AND a
  fiber whose own type refines rec — ninja::T is a rec::T, so the ninja answers a rec-typed instruction as
  itself — while ?<=lst(...) reaches neither, and ?<=int(...) reaches only an int-valued fiber
  (ex::[o=>12].plus?<=int adds at o, since the bundle is a rec, not an int).
- a named domain splits the two levels. The bundle answers as the very type it instantiates — a bracket does
  not change the name (dojo[master] is a dojo; a predicated domain additionally requires the same predicates) —
  and nothing else counts for it: not its own field bag, and not a fiber it merely borrows. A fiber answers as the
  value it holds, so a *structural* type (weaponed -> rec::T[?[weapon=>str::T]]) is also satisfied by a fiber's own
  shape: the ninja at role carrying a weapon answers ?<=weaponed(...) as itself. That is why ?<=weaponed reaches
  the ninja and never the bundle.
- the fiber bundle speaks first: when the domain NAMES a type the bundle itself is, the bundle is the subject
  and its fibers are not asked — weaponed[weaponed]::[weapon=>'axe',role=>weaponed::[weapon=>'knife']] answers
  ?<=weaponed(weapon) with 'axe' alone, not {'axe','knife'}. A domain that names no single subject — a generic
  one, or a base FORM (about every subject of that form) — does not supersede: ?<=rec and an untyped read still
  sum over both levels.
- a FILTER asks the bundle first too: a filter keeps or drops its SUBJECT, and the subject is the fibered rec —
  so *marko.?weaponed::T answers *marko (the bundle is accepted as a weaponed through the ninja it exposes; the
  filter does not also hand back the ninja). Only when the bundle declines does the filter fall through to the
  fibers, and a fail:: from the bundle still propagates.
- noobj is the multiplicity identity, so {noobj, 29} = 29: a subject the instruction is not about contributes
  nothing. A fail:: is not the identity — it PROPAGATES — or an instruction that broke on one part of the bundle
  would read as a success.
- subjects are one level deep: a fiber that is itself a bundle is applied to as the object it is, never expanded
  again.
- Inst.Form.typer — as, ::, type, vid, tid — never lifts. A typer retypes the one object it is given,
  so it is opaque: as(person::T) is both the narrowing escape from a fan-out and the exception to it (it changes the
  basis, so it cannot be distributed over the old one).
- ref-writes (<uri> -> obj) are address-precise and never lift. update (>>=) does fan out, since its domain is
  any obj; as(T) first, or ?<=T on the call, is what narrows it back to one basis.
- a fan-out result is an unordered multiplicity. When order or provenance matters the user writes the keyed rec
  explicitly — one key per fiber, each narrowing its own call ([role => *marko.describe?<=ninja(), position =>
  *marko.describe?<=position()]). There is no keyed projection that does it for you.
- a bundle on which no subject applies yields noobj — a miss is not a failure. The same miss on a non-bundle
  value is still a loud unable to locate inst-f, because there is nothing else to try.

acceptance and covariance

Two questions, and they must not be confused: *may I pass this value here* (acceptance) and *which object does this
instruction run on* (dispatch).

- A fiber named at coefficient one must be there. The value is tested against the declaration, and a field it
  does not have fails that test. Absence is legal only where the fiber's coefficient admits zero —
  rec[role,position{?}] — and reading a missing key still yields noobj. noobj is a value, not a hole.
- A predicated fiber type is satisfied by the FIBER'S VALUE. A poly entry types one of the bundle's fibers
  (person[ninja] puts a ninja at the field the declaration calls role), so the object a trait's shape is about
  (ninja::T[?[name=>str::T]]) is the value AT that fiber — bundle>>role — not the bundle's declaration. A
  *shaped nominal* trait therefore accepts a bundle that only exposes the trait-carrying fiber: the trait's shape is
  asked of bundle>>role, which is why kestrel[falconer] is a falconer although the bundle itself declares no
  name. The two fallbacks: with no value at hand (a type-vs-type question) the fiber's DECLARED type answers for its
  value, and a field the bundle's declaration itself types incompatibly (name=>str where the trait wants
  name=>int) is a veto. A field the declaration stays silent about is not a contradiction — that is exactly the case
  the fiber's value exists to answer.
- Covariance: a fibered value is acceptable where its base OR ANY fiber is expected. person[ninja] is a
  person and a ninja. The scope guard matters as much as the rule: this is rec only — lst[int] is not an
  int, and object[int] is not an int.
- Covariance is type acceptance only, never dispatch. A bundle that merely *borrows* a fiber by covariance does
  not thereby fire that fiber's instructions; the object the definition was written for is the object it runs on.
- Dispatch is an identity question: a named domain selects the subject that IS that type — the fiber whose own
  type is that name (or whose own *shape* satisfies a structural one: a ninja carrying a weapon IS a weaponed), or
  the bundle when the name is the bundle's DECLARATION (dojo[master] is a dojo). Borrowed names are not
  identities, and neither is a bundle's own field bag: the bundle is what it instantiates. |

A shaped nominal trait asks the value at the fiber, not the bundle:

acceptance is asked of the fiber's value, not the bundle's declaration
mtron> [-- the bundle declares ONLY the fiber it exposes --]
mtron> kestrel -> rec[role]::T[?[role=>rec::T]]@kestrel
mtron> [-- the shaped nominal trait declares the shape of the fiber's value --]
mtron> falconer -> rec::T[?[name=>str::T]]@falconer
mtron> jarl -> kestrel[falconer]::[role=>falconer::[name=>'sigrid']]@jarl
==>kestrel[falconer]::[role=>falconer::[name=>'sigrid']]@jarl
mtron> [-- the bundle declares no name; the falconer at role carries one, so jarl is a falconer --]
mtron> *jarl.isa(falconer::T)
==>kestrel[falconer]::[role=>falconer::[name=>'sigrid']]
mtron> [-- a fiber value that CONTRADICTS the trait's field type is refused, however the poly names it --]
mtron> skald -> kestrel[falconer]::[role=>[name=>7]]@skald
==>kestrel[falconer]::[role=>[name=>7]]@skald
mtron> *skald.isa(falconer::T)
The claim rule is what keeps the declaration/instance asymmetry valid at the uri layer:

| lhs             | rhs             | test  |
|-----------------|-----------------|-------|
| person        | person[ninja] | true  |
| person[ninja] | person        | false |
| person[ninja] | person[A]     | true  |
| person[ninja] | person[role]  | false |

worked example: two fibers

The declaration names both fibers; the instance types them. position is declared bare (rec::T@position) on
purpose — a trait declared *with* a shape asks the bundle's declaration to pass its test, and this bundle declares
name, age, role and position, not a position's title/rank:

a fibered type: the declaration names the fibers, the instance types them
mtron> person -> rec[role,position]::T[?[name=>str::T,age=>nat::T,role=>rec::T,position=>rec::T]]@person
mtron> ninja -> rec::T@ninja
mtron> position -> rec::T@position
mtron> marko -> person[ninja,position]::[name=>'marko',age=>29,role=>ninja::[name=>'dark_assassin'],position=>position::[title=>'sniper',rank=>5]]@marko
==>person[ninja,position]::[
    name=>'marko',
    age=>29,
    role=>ninja::[name=>'dark_assassin'],
    position=>position::[title=>'sniper',rank=>5]]@marko
mtron> [-- untyped: both the bundle and the role fiber carry a name --]
mtron> *marko>>name
==>'marko'
==>'dark_assassin'
mtron> [-- only the position fiber carries a title; noobj is the identity --]
mtron> *marko>>title
==>'sniper'
mtron> [-- a bundle's own field reads alone --]
mtron> *marko>>age
==>29
The instantiation is carried by the value's own type, so *marko.type() reports the DECLARATION instantiated with
both arguments — rec[role,position]::T[?[…]]@person[ninja,position] — while *marko still prints the value under
that type.

A named domain picks the subject that IS that type — the role fiber, or the position fiber, never the bundle that
merely borrows them. A body that reads a key its own fiber does not carry has nothing to answer:

dispatch is identity: a named domain reaches the fiber whose own type is that name
mtron> aim -> |inst?<=position(){ >>title }
mtron> shadow -> |inst?<=ninja(){ >>name }
mtron> *marko.aim()                    [-- dom=position: the position fiber's title --]
==>'sniper'
mtron> *marko.aim?<=position()         [-- the same call with its type named at the call site --]
==>'sniper'
mtron> *marko.shadow()                 [-- dom=ninja: the role fiber's own name, never the position's title --]
==>'dark_assassin'
An untyped call is about every subject, so an instruction both fibers declare answers twice; ?<=T narrows it, and
a typer stays on the bundle alone:

untyped fans out, ?<=T selects, a typer does not lift
mtron> describe?dom=ninja -> |inst?<=ninja(){ 'a shadow' }
mtron> describe?dom=position -> |inst?<=position(){ 'sniper report' }
mtron> *marko.describe()               [-- both fibers declare a body: an unordered multiplicity --]
==>'a shadow'
==>'sniper report'
mtron> *marko.describe?<=position()    [-- one fiber, one answer --]
==>'sniper report'
mtron> *marko.as(person::T)            [-- a typer is opaque: the bundle alone, the instantiation erased --]
==>person::[name=>'marko',
            age=>29,
            role=>ninja::[name=>'dark_assassin'],
            position=>position::[title=>'sniper',rank=>5]]

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Explain the mtron concept: type checking and casting.
output:
.test() — predicate membership

Tests whether a value satisfies a type's predicate (and nominal ancestry):

mtron> 1.isa(int::T)           [-- 1  (admitted: the value is printed) --]
==>1
mtron> 'a string'.isa(int::T)  [-- noobj  (refused: the filter prints nothing) --]
mtron> 2.isa(posint::T)        [-- 2  (admitted: 2 > 0) --]
==>2
mtron> -1.isa(posint::T)       [-- noobj  (refused: -1 is not > 0) --]
So the filter's verdict doubles as its output: admit and the value comes back, refuse and there is nothing to
print. (Refining *type against type* — "is hundreds a refinement of posint?" — is a question for the type
hierarchy, seen in *type hierarchy and refinement*.)

.as() — the cast

.as(type) is the cast: the type's predicate tests the value first, and only an admitted value is re-stamped
with the type's vid (and, if the type carries one, run through its constructor — see *type constructors* above):

mtron> [-- intabs has a constructor (absolute value), but the gate still runs first --]
mtron> 2.as(intabs::T)          [-- intabs::2  (admitted, re-stamped) --]
==>intabs::2
mtron> -2.as(intabs::T) [-- refused: -2 is not an intabs — construction (intabs::-2) is the door that coerces --]
==>fail::[inst apply failure: -2 is not a int::T[/m/inst/is(/m/inst/gt(0))][/m/inst/choose([/m/inst/is(/m/inst/lt(0))=>/m/inst/mult(-1),/m/inst/id()=>/m/inst/id()])./m/inst/rshift()]@intabs [structural] (at /m/inst/as@1)]
mtron> [-- Without a constructor the cast is a pure test --]
mtron> -2.as(int::T[?>0])  [-- fails: a lambda type, no constructor, nothing to coerce --]
==>fail::[inst apply failure: -2 is not a int::T[/m/inst/is(/m/inst/gt(0))] [structural] (at /m/inst/as@1)]
.as() is also used for nominal type casting — a rec is admitted to a nominal rec type when it nominally fits,
and the stamp records the fit:

mtron> [name=>'fuzzy feet',age=>2].as(chicken::T)    [-- chicken::[name=>'fuzzy feet',age=>2]  (nominally a being: the stamp goes on) --]
==>chicken::[name=>'fuzzy feet',age=>2]
mtron> human::[name=>'marko',age=>29].as(chicken::T)  [-- refused: a human is not a chicken, nominally --]
==>fail::[inst apply failure: human::[name=>'marko',age=>29] is not a being::T@chicken [nominal] (at /m/inst/as)]
Note the asymmetry: an anonymous rec has no lineage to contradict it, so its fields alone decide the fit — the
chicken demands age=>int::T, and the rec supplies it. A stamped human, though, carries a lineage — human
and chicken are *siblings* under being, and a sibling does not refine a sibling. Nominal fit follows the actual
refinement path, not structural overlap.

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Tell me about lowest common denominator in mtron.
output:
The most specific type that subsumes a set of types. The VM computes LCDs on the way: a mapped result over mixed
values, a rec whose fields carry different types, a poly whose members disagree — each settles on the LCD of the
pieces it is combining.

The lcd() instruction asks for one on demand over a set of related types — verified under a production VM boot:

int::T[?>1]@aa
aa::T[?>2]@bb
bb::T[?>3]@cc
aa::T[?>22]@aabb
aabb::T[?>33]@cccc
lcd(aabb::T,bb::T,cccc::T)      [-- aabb, the set's denominator --]
lcd(bb::T,cc::T)
type + type itself has no instruction — summing types is refused (the fail text you get today, shown not run):

posint::T + hundreds::T         [-- fail: int::T[is(gt(0))]@posint [type] unable to convert int::T (at plus) --]

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Define the space these examples use as used in mtron.
output:
Every block below runs against one sqlite database mounted as tbledoc:#. (mtron_pre blocks are executed by the
docs pipeline and inlined with their results; a plain mtron block is only shown.)

mtron> import(/m/db/tble)
mtron> tblespace::[pattern => tbledoc:#,
                   host    => <sqlite:/tmp/mtron-tbledoc.db>,
                   driver  => <org.sqlite.JDBC>,
                   q       => [incrq::[=>],
                               docq::[tbledoc:person => docs::[
                                 desc    => "a person row: name, age, and a skill once one is written",
                                 example => ["*tbledoc:person/+.count()"]]]],
                   route   => [tbledoc: => <>]]@/sys/space/tbledoc
The two q entries are the space's query processors, and both earn their place: docq is what lets *a space
document its own tables* — so ?docq on a table tells an agent what it is looking at before it queries it — and incrq
is what makes a _?incrq write assign its own key (see *keys the database assigns* below).

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
output:
| type           | vid                                  | tid        | meaning                                                             |
|----------------|--------------------------------------|------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| tblespace::T | /m/db/tble/space/tblespace            | space::T | a JDBC database as a space; isa rec[host=>uri::T,driver=>uri::T]  |
| table types    | /sys/space/<space>/instset/<table> | rec::T   | one per discovered table, published into the space's schema instset |

mtron> *tblespace?docq      [-- the type, its ctor, and the space's own summary --]
==>docs::[obj=>/m/space::T[?[host=>uri::T,driver=>uri::T]][ctor?tblespace<=(rec::T){<j>}]@/m/db/tble/space/tblespace,
          desc=>'[structural] a metatron realizatio...',
          example=>['*<http://metatron.phaseshift.studi...']]
mtron> *</m/db/tble/helper>    [-- the instset's helper rec: the llm chat schema, as a str --]
==>[llm_chat_schema=>inst?<=#{*}(){<j>}]

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
output:
| key          | type     | meaning                                                                                                              |
|--------------|----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| pattern    | uri::T | the uri subtree this space owns — tbledoc:#                                                                        |
| host       | uri::T | the JDBC url without its jdbc: prefix: <sqlite:/tmp/x.db>, <postgresql://host:5432/db?user=..&password=..> |
| driver     | uri::T | the JDBC driver class — <org.sqlite.JDBC>, <org.postgresql.Driver>, <org.mariadb.jdbc.Driver>                  |
| route      | rec::T | scheme → path inside the space: [tbledoc: => <>] strips the scheme; a value can point a subtree elsewhere          |
| q          | rec::T | query processors — incrq::[=>] for _?incrq key assignment, docq to document tables (above)                     |
| serializer | uri::T | the serializer the key/value side uses; defaults to mtron's own                                                      |
| table      | lst::T | deprecated and ignored — table mapping is always on (older boot files still carry table => [,])                |

Two practical notes: sqlite will not create the parent directory of the database file, so it must already exist; and
mariadb/mysql hosts carry their credentials in the uri. A space may also be built by the ctor alone —
tblespace::[host=>..,driver=>..] — and mounted at any vid.

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Tell me about writing rows — the table appears from the first write in mtron.
output:
There is no DDL to write. The first rec written to a collection creates the table from the rec's fields; the vid's
last segment becomes the primary key; and a field the table has never seen widens the table (ALTER TABLE) and the
collection's type with it.

mtron> tbledoc:person/1 -> [name=>'marko',age=>29]
==>[name=>'marko',age=>29]
mtron> tbledoc:person/2 -> [name=>'grant',age=>25]
==>[name=>'grant',age=>25]
mtron> tbledoc:person/3 -> [name=>'metis',age=>41]
==>[name=>'metis',age=>41]
mtron> tbledoc:person/4 -> [name=>'xilo',age=>33,skill=>'graph']    [-- a field the table has not seen --]
==>[name=>'xilo',age=>33,skill=>'graph']
SQL column types follow the obj types, and the column catalog is readable as data — _mtron_meta is where metatron
keeps what SQL cannot say:

mtron> */sys/space/tbledoc.sql('SELECT table_name, column_name, base_vid, obj_tid, ref_table FROM _mtron_meta')
==>[table_name=>'person',
    column_name=>'$table',
    base_vid=>'/m/rec',
    obj_tid=>'/m/rec']
==>[table_name=>'person',
    column_name=>'name',
    base_vid=>'/m/str',
    obj_tid=>'/m/str']
==>[table_name=>'person',
    column_name=>'age',
    base_vid=>'/m/int',
    obj_tid=>'/m/int']
==>[table_name=>'person',
    column_name=>'skill',
    base_vid=>'/m/str',
    obj_tid=>'/m/str']
A structural obj (tags=>['a','b']) rides in a TEXT column with its type preserved in obj_tid, so a read
reconstructs the lst rather than a string that looks like one.

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Define reading rows as used in mtron.
output:
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+              [-- every row as a rec --]
==>[name=>'xilo',age=>33,skill=>'graph']
==>[name=>'marko',age=>29]
==>[name=>'metis',age=>41]
==>[name=>'grant',age=>25]
mtron> *tbledoc:person/1              [-- one row --]
==>[name=>'marko',age=>29]
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+/             [-- vid => row --]
==>tbledoc:person/4=>[name=>'xilo',age=>33,skill=>'graph']
==>tbledoc:person/1=>[name=>'marko',age=>29]
==>tbledoc:person/3=>[name=>'metis',age=>41]
==>tbledoc:person/2=>[name=>'grant',age=>25]
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+/name         [-- one column, across rows --]
==>'metis'
==>'grant'
==>'marko'
==>'xilo'
mtron> *tbledoc:person/1/name         [-- one field: the row is unrolled --]
==>'marko'
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+/id           [-- the keys: they live in the vid, not in the body --]
==>1
==>2
==>4
==>3
Rows come back in whatever order the backend chose — say so in the expression (.order(select(col))) when position
matters.

anchor vs clone: who keeps the address

* is a clone and @ is an anchor, and for a table row that is the difference between a value and an
*addressable* value. Take the fields out of the rows and the clone loses the row it came from:

mtron> *tbledoc:person/+/+      [-- clone: fields detached from their rows --]
==>'metis'
==>41
==>'grant'
==>25
==>33
==>29
==>'graph'
==>'marko'
==>'xilo'
mtron> @tbledoc:person/+/+      [-- anchor: the same fields, each still addressed to its row --]
==>'metis'@tbledoc:person/3/name
==>41@tbledoc:person/3/age
==>'grant'@tbledoc:person/2/name
==>25@tbledoc:person/2/age
==>33@tbledoc:person/4/age
==>29@tbledoc:person/1/age
==>'graph'@tbledoc:person/4/skill
==>'marko'@tbledoc:person/1/name
==>'xilo'@tbledoc:person/4/name
The same holds for a rewrite's result — it is the clone path that hands rows back with a placeholder vid, which is why
the anchored form is the one to keep when the rows might be written back:

mtron> *tbledoc:person/+.take(2)     [-- clone path --]
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/person::[
    name=>'marko',
    age=>29]@tbledoc:person/1
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/person::[
    name=>'grant',
    age=>25]@tbledoc:person/2
mtron> @tbledoc:person/+.take(2)     [-- anchor path --]
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/person::[
    name=>'marko',
    age=>29]@tbledoc:person/1
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/person::[
    name=>'grant',
    age=>25]@tbledoc:person/2

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: What is the rewrites — reads that become SQL in mtron?
output:
The interesting half of /m/db/tble: a read that matches a table is rewritten to SQL before it runs, so count() is
SELECT COUNT(*), isa() is WHERE, and a projection is a column list. The match is on the *code*, not the data — the
same expression over a memspace stays in mtron.

mtron> *tbledoc:person/+.?[age=>?<30]        [-- SELECT * FROM person WHERE age < 30 --]
==>[name=>'marko',
    age=>29]@tbledoc:person/noobj
==>[name=>'grant',
    age=>25]@tbledoc:person/noobj
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+.count()               [-- SELECT COUNT(*) FROM person --]
==>4
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+/age.sum()             [-- SELECT SUM(age) FROM person --]
==>128
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+/age.mean()            [-- SELECT AVG(age) FROM person --]
==>32.0
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+.==[name=>_]           [-- SELECT name FROM person --]
==>[name=>'xilo']
==>[name=>'marko']
==>[name=>'metis']
==>[name=>'grant']
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+.order(select(age))    [-- ... ORDER BY age --]
==>[[
     name=>'grant',
     age=>25]@tbledoc:person/noobj,
    [
     name=>'marko',
     age=>29]@tbledoc:person/noobj,
    [
     name=>'xilo',
     age=>33,
     skill=>'graph']@tbledoc:person/noobj,
    [
     name=>'metis',
     age=>41]@tbledoc:person/noobj]
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+.dedup(select(name))   [-- SELECT DISTINCT name FROM person --]
==>'marko'
==>'grant'
==>'metis'
==>'xilo'
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+.take(2)               [-- ... LIMIT 2 --]
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/person::[
    name=>'marko',
    age=>29]@tbledoc:person/1
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/person::[
    name=>'grant',
    age=>25]@tbledoc:person/2
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+.skip(1)               [-- ... OFFSET 1 --]
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/person::[
    name=>'grant',
    age=>25]@tbledoc:person/2
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/person::[
    name=>'metis',
    age=>41]@tbledoc:person/3
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/person::[
    name=>'xilo',
    age=>33,
    skill=>'graph']@tbledoc:person/4
| rewrite                  | mtron                                   | sql                                                 |
|--------------------------|-----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| sql_where              | *db:table/+/+.?[col=>pred]          | SELECT * ... WHERE                                |
| sql_where_count        | *db:table/+/+.?[col=>pred].count()  | SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE                         |
| sql_where_order        | ...?[..].order(select(col))         | ... WHERE ... ORDER BY                            |
| sql_where_order_offset | ...?[..].order(select(col)).skip(n) | ... ORDER BY ... OFFSET n                         |
| sql_where_limit        | ...?[..].take(n)                    | ... WHERE ... LIMIT n                             |
| sql_where_offset       | ...?[..].skip(n)                    | ... WHERE ... OFFSET n                            |
| sql_where_offset_limit | ...?[..].skip(m).take(n)            | ... WHERE ... LIMIT n OFFSET m                    |
| sql_select             | *db:table/+/+.==[col=>_]              | SELECT col ...                                    |
| sql_order              | *db:table/+/+.order(select(col))      | ... ORDER BY col                                  |
| sql_distinct           | *db:table/+/+.dedup(select(col))      | SELECT DISTINCT col ...                           |
| sql_count              | *db:table/+/+.count()                 | SELECT COUNT(*)                                   |
| sql_sum                | *db:table/+/col.sum()                 | SELECT SUM(col)                                   |
| sql_mean               | *db:table/+/col.mean()                | SELECT AVG(col)                                   |
| sql_limit              | *db:table/+/+.take(n)                 | ... LIMIT n                                       |
| sql_offset             | *db:table/+/+.skip(n)                 | ... OFFSET n                                      |
| sql_offset_limit       | *db:table/+/+.skip(m).take(n)         | ... LIMIT n OFFSET m                              |
| kv_count               | *db:kv/+.count()                      | SELECT COUNT(*) FROM kv_store WHERE furi LIKE ... |
| kv_limit               | *db:kv/+.take(n)                      | ... LIMIT n (broken on the typed schema — below)  |

The instset prints that list itself, and each rewrite documents its own before/after code:

mtron> */m/db/tble?docq
==>docs::[obj=>/m/instset::[
           pattern=>/m/db/tble/#,
           q=>[
            docq::[
             pattern=>docq,
             pre_read=>inst(uri::T){<j>},
             pre_write=>inst(uri::T,#::T){<j>},
             obj=>memspace::[pattern=><#>],
             inst=>/m/instset::[=>]],
            /m/qproc/decq::[
             pattern=>decq,
             pre_read=>inst(uri::T){<j>},
             pre_write=>inst(uri::T,#::T){<j>},
             obj=>/m/instset::[=>]]],
           const=>[[llm_chat_schema=>inst?<=#{*}(){<j>}]@/m/web/helper],
           type=>[/m/space::T[?[host=>uri::T,driver=>uri::T]][ctor?tblespace<=(rec::T){<j>}]@/m/db/tble/space/tblespace],
           inst=>[sql?rec{*}<=tblespace(str::T){<j>}],
           rewrite=>[
            /m/db/tble/inst/rewrite/sql_count?code{?}<=code(){<j>},
            /m/db/tble/inst/rewrite/sql_sum?code{?}<=code(){<j>},
            /m/db/tble/inst/rewrite/sql_sum_column?code{?}<=code(){<j>},
            /m/db/tble/inst/rewrite/sql_mean?code{?}<=code(){<j>},
            /m/db/tble/inst/rewrite/sql_limit?code{?}<=code(){<j>},
            /m/db/tble/inst/rewrite/sql_offset?code{?}<=code(){<j>},
            /m/db/tble/inst/rewrite/sql_offset_limit?code{?}<=code(){<j>},
            ...(12 more)]]@/m/db/tble,
          desc=>'relational tables, typed rows, and...',
          example=>['*acme:customer.where[person=>[name...']]
when a read stays in mtron

The match is structural and it DECLINES rather than guesses, so a read that names a table can still run in the VM. Each
of these is a deliberate fall-back, not a silent downgrade — explain() shows which one happened:

* the predicate does not fit the formatter — a non-rec predicate, a wildcard field (_, +), or a value that is
  not a uri/int/real/str/bool/comparison (a call, a variable, a nested rec). The where rewrite leaves the pair alone
  and the rows are filtered in mtron.
* the collection is not a real table — a kv_store path (see kv_count/kv_limit above) or a wildcard collection.
  where/count/take match only a collection that the discovered schema actually holds, so the key/value rules
  handle the kv form and nothing else pushes down.
* the read is not a plain row multiplicity — count() after a field or an extension (e.g. *db:table/+/name.count()
  is a count of *distinct names*, i.e. SELECT COUNT(name)) does not match the row-count rule; it is a different
  question, not a missed optimization.

A fused op is only fused because the space could be resolved from it: sql_where stores the address as the from
instruction wrote it (db:table/+), and every sql_where_* rule resolves the space from that address before it agrees
to fuse. An arg that no longer names a space is a rule that declines, quietly.

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Explain the mtron concept: native sql.
output:
When the vocabulary is not enough, go to the backend. sql takes a str — templates included — and yields rec{*},
which mtron then treats like any other objs.

mtron> */sys/space/tbledoc.sql('SELECT name, age FROM person WHERE age < 30')
==>[name=>'marko',age=>29]
==>[name=>'grant',age=>25]
mtron> */sys/space/tbledoc.sql('SELECT name, age FROM person WHERE age < 30')>>age.sum()
==>54
A sql str may carry several statements: all but the last run as updates, the last is the query whose result set comes
back. Templates reach the graph, so a query can be parameterized by live state — the instruction's own example is
sql('SELECT * FROM movie WHERE runtime < ${*next_event} - time(now)').

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Tell me about foreign keys: a !* in the cell in mtron.
output:
auto_from is metatron's structural foreign key: the pointer is part of the row value, and it stays lazy until a
traversal forces the read. Where a where-join computes a relationship at query time, a !* cell *is* the
relationship.

mtron> tbledoc:award/1 -> [trophy=>'gold',recipient=>!*tbledoc:person/1]
==>[trophy=>'gold',
    recipient=>!*tbledoc:person/1]
mtron> tbledoc:award/2 -> [trophy=>'silver',recipient=>!*tbledoc:person/2]
==>[trophy=>'silver',
    recipient=>!*tbledoc:person/2]
mtron> *tbledoc:award/+                [-- the cell renders as an unresolved pointer --]
==>[trophy=>'silver',
    recipient=>!*tbledoc:person/2]
==>[trophy=>'gold',
    recipient=>!*tbledoc:person/1]
mtron> *tbledoc:award/1/recipient      [-- traversal resolves it to the row --]
==>[name=>'marko',age=>29]
The SQL footprint is deliberately plain: the column is a bare INTEGER (TEXT for string keys), there is no SQL
FOREIGN KEY constraint, and the pointer metadata — including ref_table — lives in _mtron_meta. An intra-space
pointer stores the bare table name; an inter-space pointer (!*mem:venue/1 into a memspace, a grphspace, an
fsSpace…) keeps its scheme and routes through the router, so a row can point anywhere in the metatron graph. Both
kinds may sit in one row.

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Define the schema of what you are querying as used in mtron.
output:
mtron> */sys/space/tbledoc/schema/pattern      [-- where the discovered types are published --]
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/#
mtron> */sys/space/tbledoc/instset/+/          [-- the types as addressed objs --]
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/person=>rec::T[?[{?}name=>str::T,
            {?}age=>int::T,
            {?}skill=>str::T,
            uri::T=><#>::T]]@/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/person
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/award=>rec::T[?[{?}trophy=>str::T,
            recipient=>isa(person/+/id).!*id(),
            uri::T=><#>::T]]@/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/award
Reading the schema is how you meet a table you have never seen: each entry is an isa([{?}name=>str::T,…]) refinement
of rec::T, and a foreign-key column appears as recipient=>isa(person/+/id).!*id() — the column *is* the pointer.
A table's type is replaced when the table widens.

Discovery is lazy, and it is worth knowing exactly what fires it: the catalog walk runs on the first *write*, or on
a read of the space's instset (*/sys/space/<space>/instset/+/). Until it has run, the space does not know which
collections are tables, so a table read falls through to the key/value side and comes back empty — a freshly mounted
space answers 0 to a count that the database file can prove is not zero (see *taking the space down* below).

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: What is the key/value fall-through — and documents in mtron?
output:
kv, kv_store, msg and _mtron_meta are the reserved collections. A write to a reserved path is stored as a
typed key/value entry — same database, no table — and a nested rec turns that corner into a document store:

mtron> tbledoc:kv/greeting -> 'salve, metatron'
==>'salve, metatron'
mtron> *tbledoc:kv/greeting
==>'salve, metatron'
mtron> tbledoc:kv/session/1 -> [user=>'marko',cart=>['fig','olive']]
==>[user=>'marko',cart=>['fig','olive']]
mtron> *tbledoc:kv/session/1/cart      [-- a field of the stored document --]
==>['fig','olive']
mtron> *tbledoc:kv/+/                  [-- vid => value --]
==>tbledoc:kv/greeting=>'salve, metatron'

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Explain the mtron concept: patching a row (a write replaces it).
output:
A write to an existing key replaces the row body — fields left out of the rec are cleared:

mtron> tbledoc:person/5 -> [name=>'vela',age=>52]
==>[name=>'vela',age=>52]
mtron> tbledoc:person/5 -> [age=>53]        [-- a partial write: name is cleared --]
==>[age=>53]
mtron> *tbledoc:person/5
==>[age=>53]
To patch, anchor the row and update it in place. >>= [k=>v] overlays fields the row already has; +[k=>v] promotes a
field it does not (creating the column, if the table has never had one):

mtron> @tbledoc:person/5 >>= +[name=>'vela']     [-- set promotion --]
==>[age=>53,name=>'vela']
mtron> *tbledoc:person/5
==>[name=>'vela',age=>53]

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Tell me about keys the database assigns in mtron.
output:
_ as the last path segment asks the backend for the key — the uri says *where the row lives in the table*, the
database says *what its key is*. Two things have to be true for it to work: the space must declare the incrq query
processor (q => [incrq::[=>]], in the setup block above), and the write must ask for it with ?incrq:

mtron> tbledoc:note/_?incrq -> [body=>'a note with a database-assigned key']
==>[body=>'a note with a database-assigned key']@tbledoc:note/1
mtron> tbledoc:note/_?incrq -> [body=>'another one']
==>[body=>'another one']@tbledoc:note/2
mtron> *tbledoc:note/+/id                                    [-- the keys the backend picked --]
==>1
==>2

instruction: Answer this question about the mtron language and metatron virtual machine accurately and concisely.
input: Define taking the space down as used in mtron.
output:
A space is a mount, not a copy. Writing noobj to its vid takes it down: the pattern stops routing, the JDBC
connection closes, and the schema instset the space published goes with it. The rows do not — they live in the database
file, so mounting a tblespace over the same file brings them back. The block below is also the shortest proof of how
lazy that mount is: the rows are there from the first statement, but the space only learns they are *tables* when
something walks the catalog:

mtron> /sys/space/tbledoc -> noobj                 [-- unmount --]
mtron> tblespace::[pattern => tbledoc:#,
                   host    => <sqlite:/tmp/mtron-tbledoc.db>,
                   driver  => <org.sqlite.JDBC>,
                   route   => [tbledoc: => <>]]@/sys/space/tbledoc
mtron> *tbledoc:person/+.count()                   [-- 0: a fresh mount has not discovered its tables yet --]
==>5
mtron> */sys/space/tbledoc/instset/+/              [-- reading the instset is what walks the catalog --]
==>/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/award=>rec::T[?[{?}trophy=>str::T,
            recipient=>isa(person/+/id).!*id()]]@/sys/space/tbledoc/instset/award

datetime::T (/m/math/datetime)

structure

datetime::T is a uri::T refinement with this layout:

//yyyy.MM:dd/HH/mm/ss/SSS?tz=±HHmm
| component | uri field       | range   | description     |
|-----------|-----------------|---------|-----------------|
| year      | host (pre-.)  | 0000+   | calendar year   |
| month     | host (post-.) | 01–12   | month           |
| day       | port            | 01–31   | day of month    |
| hour      | path[-4]        | 00–23   | hour            |
| minute    | path[-3]        | 00–59   | minute          |
| second    | path[-2]        | 00–59   | second          |
| millis    | path[-1]        | 000–999 | millisecond     |
| tz        | q tz          | ±HHMM   | timezone offset |

construction

mtron> [-- current system time --]
mtron> datetime_now()
==>datetime::<//2026.11:722/07/02/896?tz=Z>
mtron> [-- from record (goes through .as(uri::T) first) --]
mtron> [host=><2024.12>,port=>25,path=>[<>,<09>,<00>,<00>,<000>],
        c=>[min=>1,max=>1],q=>[tz=>'-0500']].as(uri::T).as(datetime::T)
==>datetime::<//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>
mtron> [-- from string-encoded URI --]
mtron> <//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>.as(datetime::T)
==>datetime::<//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>
typed vs bare uris

Bare URIs like <//2024.12:25/...> work with standard URI operations (>>host, >>port, >>path). The datetime
vocabulary (year, month, day, etc.) only works on explicitly typed datetimes:

mtron> [-- rec projections of uri components --]
mtron> <//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>.as(rec::T)>>host
==><2024.12>
mtron> <//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>.as(rec::T)>>port
==>25
mtron> [-- vocabulary projections require datetime::T typing --]
mtron> datetime::<//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>>>year
==>2024
mtron> datetime::<//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>>>month
==>12
mtron> datetime::<//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>>>day
==>25
mtron> datetime::<//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>>>tz
==>'-0500'
vocabulary keys

Named >> projections for typed datetimes:

| key      | value type | source             |
|----------|------------|--------------------|
| year   | int::T   | host.split(".")[0] |
| month  | int::T   | host.split(".")[1] |
| day    | int::T   | port               |
| hour   | int::T   | path[-4]           |
| minute | int::T   | path[-3]           |
| second | int::T   | path[-2]           |
| millis | int::T   | path[-1]           |
| tz     | str::T   | q("tz")            |

Non-vocabulary keys fall through to standard URI projections.

mtron> datetime::<//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>>>{year,month,day}
==>2024
==>12
==>25
mtron> datetime::<//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>.as(rec::T)>>host
==><2024.12>
predicate validation

The datetime::T predicate ensures base uri has:

- no scheme (or empty)
- host matches \d{4}\.\d{2} with month 01–12
- port in 1–31
- path has ≥4 integer segments with valid hour (0–23), minute (0–59), second (0–59)
- query contains tz key

mtron> <//2024.13:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>.?datetime::T [-- month 13 (bad)   --]
mtron> <//2024.12:25/09/60/00/000?tz=-0500>.?datetime::T [-- second 60 (bad)  --]
mtron> <//2024.12:25/09/00/00>.?datetime::T              [-- missing tz (bad) --]
mutating and filtering

All standard uri operations apply: == (select), ? (is), plus >>= (rec update) after .as(rec::T).

mtron> [-- select mutation: change day --]
mtron> <//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>.as(rec::T)==[port=>31]>>port
==>31
mtron> [-- where filter: match day 25 --]
mtron> <//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>.as(rec::T)?[port=>25]
==>[host=><2024.12>,
    port=>25,
    authority=><2024.12:25>,
    path=>[<>,<09>,<00>,<00>,<000>],
    c=>[min=>1,max=>1],
    q=>[tz=>'-0500']]
mtron> <//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>.as(rec::T)?[port=>26]
mtron> [-- rec update: change timezone --]
mtron> <//2024.12:25/09/00/00/000?tz=-0500>.as(rec::T)>>=[q=>[tz=>'+0000']]>>q>>tz
==>'+0000'
